newsitem.title: UK: Sleaze row dominates British election campaign.
newsitem.headline: Sleaze row dominates British election campaign.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major fought back on Friday against new charges that he ignored sleaze in his Conservative Party, dismissing newspaper accusations as "total junk".
But the bitter row over the allegations of influence-peddling dominated the campaign for the May 1 election, deepening the gloom cast by the ruling party's low -- and falling -- opinion poll ratings.

Major, whose "Honest John" reputation is his party's best hope for a comback, dismissed allegations in the Guardian newspaper that he allowed MP Tim Smith to continue as junior Northern Ireland minister in 1994 after he was told that Smith took money to ask questions for businessmen in parliament.

Major, on the hustings at the start of the longest election campaign in Britain in 80 years, said he had ordered an investigation as soon as he had heard of the allegations, and Smith had quit as soon as the inquiry was finished.
"It's not a fresh matter," Major said, calling the Guardian report -- based on secret evidence given to parliament's ethics commissioner, Sir Gordon Downey -- "nonsense".
Major's office also issued details of Major's diary for October 1994, the crucial period of the affair, and of reports he made to parliament to show he had nothing to hide.

But the opposition Labour party drove home its advantage, demanding publication of a report into the so-called "cash-for-questions" scandal before the May 1 election and accusing Major of trying to avoid embarrassment with a cover-up.
"The real scandal is not that the Tory (Conservative) party has some MPs who have been accused of financial impropriety," said Labour's foreign affairs spokesman Robin Cook.
"But (it is) that the Tory leadership has consistently responded by protecting their party from being embarrassed rather than defending parliament from being corrupted."
Adding a new twist on Friday, the parliamentary ethics commissioner himself joined in the row, condemning the Guardian for leaking parts of his inquiry.
Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine seized on this, saying Downey's comments "totally vindicate everything the Government has been saying in defence of natural justice".

But there was little sign voters were sympathetic to the government. A poll in Friday's Independent newspaper showed Labour's lead over the Conservatives, bidding for a record fifth successive term, grew to 27 points from 25 a week ago.
The Guardian's allegations centre on the fact Conservative MP Tim Smith was appointed a minister in January 1994.

This, it said, was despite the fact Smith told Major's parliamentary business manager four years earlier that he had been paid by Mohammed Al-Fayed, the owner of London's upmarket store, Harrods, to ask questions on his behalf in parliament.

Major was told of the allegations in September 1994, it said. But Smith only quit his post on October 20 saying he had been foolish and mistaken not to register the payments, but denying firmly that taking the money had been wrong or corrupt.
Major, announcing the election on Monday, ordered parliament's closure on Friday, launching a six-week campaign.

But the closure effectively buried, at least until after the election, a report by the ethics watchdog into the alleged payments by Al-Fayed and payments made as election expenses to several MPs by a parliamentary lobbyist, Ian Greer.

Labour, which has called on Major to bring parliament back to hear the report, on Friday broadened its attack, calling for a probe into the ruling party's secret funding arrangements and promising tougher rules of conduct for ministers.
